analogy.p: Imagine electrons as people walking down a corridor, with the ions as obstacles they bump into. A longer corridor has more obstacles, so the journey is harder and takes more effort, just as a longer wire has more resistance. If the corridor is made wider (a thicker wire), people can find more routes round the obstacles, so the resistance goes down. The analogy breaks down because real ions are fixed in a lattice and vibrate, and the vibration increases when the wire is hot, which makes the corridor 'more crowded' as the temperature rises.

bullets: **Aim**: investigate the relationship between **length of a wire** and its **resistance**.
**Independent variable**: length of wire (measured between the crocodile clips, in cm or m).
**Dependent variable**: resistance (ohms), calculated from V and I.
**Control variables**: same wire (material and thickness/cross-sectional area), same cell p.d., same temperature.
**Hypothesis**: the longer the wire, the greater the resistance (directly proportional).
The measurements are of **p.d. (V)** and **current (A)**; resistance is **calculated**, not measured directly.
Know the answer to the question 'why is the circuit set up like this?': ammeter in series to measure current, voltmeter in parallel to measure p.d. across the wire.
core.h: What the practical investigates and why
core.p: This **required practical** investigates **how the resistance of a wire depends on its length**, at constant temperature. The aim is to measure the current through a test wire and the potential difference across it for different lengths, calculate the resistance each time using **R = V / I**, and then plot a graph of resistance against length. The result you must be able to describe and explain is that **resistance is directly proportional to length**: doubling the length doubles the resistance. The same circuit is a standard method for finding the resistance of any component.

bullets: **Ammeter**: in series, to measure the current through the wire.
**Voltmeter**: in parallel across the wire, to measure the p.d. across it.
**Switch**: lets you break the circuit between readings so the wire does not heat up.
**Metre rule**: used to measure the length of wire between the clips.
Use a **low p.d. (about 1.5 V to 2 V)** so the current stays small.
Wire: constantan or nichrome is often used because its resistance changes little with temperature.
Draw the circuit with a complete loop and standard symbols to earn full marks.
core.p: You need a **cell or low-voltage power supply**, a **switch**, an **ammeter**, a **voltmeter**, a **length of test wire** (often constantan or nichrome of known thickness), a **metre rule**, **crocodile clips** and connecting leads. The ammeter is connected **in series** with the wire so the same current flows through both, and the voltmeter is connected **in parallel across the test wire only**, between the two crocodile clips, so that it measures the p.d. across just the length being tested. The wire should be taped straight to the metre rule so the length between the clips can be read accurately.

bullets: 1. Set up the circuit as in the diagram and check all connections are tight.
2. Measure the length of wire between the clips with the metre rule; start with a short length such as 10 cm.
3. **Close the switch**, read the ammeter and voltmeter, and record the values.
4. **Open the switch immediately** to avoid the wire heating.
5. Increase the length by 10 cm and repeat, up to 100 cm.
6. Calculate **R = V / I** for every length.
7. Repeat the experiment and calculate a **mean resistance** for each length.
8. Plot a graph of resistance (y axis) against length (x axis).
core.p: Set up the circuit with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the test wire. Attach the wire to the metre rule and connect one clip at the 0 cm mark and the second clip at 10 cm. Close the switch, then **read the current and the p.d. quickly**, and open the switch again. Move the second clip to 20 cm, then to 30 cm, and so on up to 100 cm, recording V and I for each length. Repeat the whole set of readings at least once more, then calculate resistance for each length and find the mean.

bullets: Control: same **material**, same **diameter (cross-sectional area)**, same **cell p.d.**.
Control temperature: **switch off between readings**, use a low p.d., allow the wire to cool.
Hazard: **hot wire** may cause burns; avoid touching it while current flows.
Hazard: damaged leads or wet hands near electrics can cause electric shock; check leads and keep water away.
Use a **resistance wire** such as constantan because its resistance is less sensitive to temperature.
Make sure the wire is **straight** and not coiled; a coiled wire heats up faster and gives a wrong length.
Avoid contact with a hot wire; allow it to cool for several minutes.
core.p: For a fair test, only the **length** of the wire may change. **Temperature** is the key control variable, because the resistance of a metal wire increases as it heats up (the ions vibrate more and collide with electrons more often). If the wire gets hot, the results are not reliable. So use a **low current**, keep the circuit **switched off between readings**, and take readings quickly. A wire that heats up can burn skin or damage the equipment, so it is also a **safety risk**; do not touch the wire while the current is flowing and allow it to cool before handling.

bullets: Cell: long line is the positive terminal; **conventional current** flows from positive round the circuit to negative.
Ammeter: connect in **series**, in the main loop, so the same current passes through it as through the wire.
Voltmeter: connect in **parallel** with the test wire only, from clip to clip.
Fixed resistor and test wire are both drawn as a rectangle; a **variable resistor** is a rectangle with an arrow through it.
Draw circuit lines with a ruler, with no gaps, and put the symbols on the lines, not in the middle of a corner.
Connect the voltmeter last so the main series circuit is complete before the parallel branch is added.
Check the meters read zero when the switch is open: a reading shows a **zero error** to subtract from every result.
core.h: Circuit symbols and connecting the meters correctly
core.p: The practical circuit must be drawn with standard circuit symbols: a **cell** (long line positive, short line negative), a **switch**, a **fixed resistor or test wire** (a rectangle), an **ammeter** (a circle containing A) and a **voltmeter** (a circle containing V). The **ammeter goes in series** because it must measure the current that flows through the wire, so all the charge has to pass through it. The **voltmeter goes in parallel** across the component because it measures the difference in potential between two points, so it must be connected to the two ends of the wire that you are measuring. If the voltmeter were put in series it would have a very large resistance and almost no current would flow.

bullets: Table headings must include the **quantity and unit**, e.g. 'Resistance (ohm)'.
Use **R = V / I**; V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms.
Convert mA to A (divide by 1000) if the ammeter reads in milliamps.
Mean = sum of repeat values / number of repeats.
Exclude anomalies from the mean and say you did so.
Record **all repeated readings**, not just the mean.
Number of significant figures in the answer should not exceed that of the data.
core.p: Draw a results table with columns for length (cm), p.d. (V), current (A) and resistance (ohms), and include repeats and a mean. Calculate the resistance using **R = V / I**, rearranged from V = I x R. Show the calculation for at least one row to earn working marks. Calculate **mean resistance** by adding the repeat values and dividing by the number of repeats, but **ignore any anomalous result** (one that does not fit the pattern) in the mean. Give resistance to a sensible number of significant figures, consistent with the readings.

bullets: Label axes with quantity and unit; choose a scale that uses more than half the grid.
Draw a **straight line of best fit** through the origin; it need not pass through every point.
Direct proportion: **doubling the length doubles the resistance**.
Gradient = change in R / change in L = **resistance per unit length**.
A line that does not pass through the origin suggests a **systematic error**, such as contact resistance at the clips or a zero error on the meters.
Use the graph to read off an unknown length or resistance (interpolation).
Conclusion: 'resistance is directly proportional to the length of the wire at constant temperature'.
core.p: Plot **resistance on the y axis and length on the x axis**. The points should lie close to a **straight line that passes through the origin**, drawn with a ruler as a line of best fit (some points can lie above and some below). A straight line through the origin shows that **resistance is directly proportional to length**. The **gradient** equals R / L, which is the resistance per unit length (ohms per cm or per m) for that wire. You can use the line to predict the resistance of a length you did not test, and to check for anomalies.

bullets: Electrons are the charge carriers in a metal.
Collisions with **ions** cause resistance and transfer energy to the thermal store of the wire.
**Longer wire = more ions in the path = more collisions = more resistance**.
**Thicker wire** (larger cross-sectional area) has more paths for the electrons, so **less resistance**.
**Higher temperature** means more ion vibration and more collisions, so resistance increases.
The relationship between length and resistance is **directly proportional**, not just 'increases'.
Say 'electrons collide with ions' or 'lattice', not 'atoms get in the way' to be precise.
core.p: Current in a metal wire is a flow of **electrons**. As the electrons move along the wire they **collide with the vibrating positive ions** in the lattice, which transfers energy and opposes the flow of charge; this opposition is **resistance**. In a longer wire there are **more ions** in the path, so the electrons collide more often and the resistance is greater. A wire that is twice as long has twice as many ions to collide with in series, so it has twice the resistance, which is why resistance is proportional to length. The same idea explains why resistance increases at higher temperature: the ions vibrate more, so collisions are more frequent.

bullets: Use at least **five lengths** over as wide a range as possible, for example 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm.
Take the length from the **inside edges of the clips**, with your eye directly above the scale to avoid **parallax error**.
**Resolution** of the metre rule is 1 mm; of a typical digital meter is the last digit shown.
Choose the **range** of each meter so the pointer or display uses most of the scale (for example 0 to 1 A, not 0 to 10 A).
A **repeat** reading means measuring the same length again; a **replicate** set means doing the whole experiment again.
Anomalous results should be **checked by repeating**, not simply deleted.
A larger range of lengths makes the gradient of the graph more precise, because a small error in one point matters less.
core.p: Good practical technique means choosing readings that give a clear pattern. A set of lengths from 10 cm to 100 cm in equal steps gives at least five different values of the independent variable, which is enough to draw a convincing straight-line graph. The **resolution** of an instrument is the smallest change in the quantity that it can show. A metre rule with 1 mm divisions has a resolution of 1 mm, so measuring the length to the nearest millimetre is sensible; a digital ammeter with two decimal places reads to 0.01 A. Using a **low p.d.** keeps the current small, which stops the wire heating, but the current must still be large enough to read clearly on the meter.

bullets: **Heating of the wire**: use a low current, switch off between readings.
**Contact resistance** at the clips adds extra resistance; clean the clips and press them firmly on the wire.
**Zero error** on the ammeter or voltmeter shifts all results; check the meter reads zero before starting.
**Parallax error** when reading the ruler: view from directly above.
**Wire not straight** gives a wrong length.
**Repeat readings** and calculate a mean to reduce random error; identify anomalies.
Use a digital meter with a high resolution to improve the accuracy of readings.
core.h: Sources of error and improving reliability
core.p: Errors fall into **random errors**, which change unpredictably from reading to reading, and **systematic errors**, which shift every result in the same direction. In this practical the main random error is reading the length against the rule, and the main systematic errors are **contact resistance at the crocodile clips** and **heating of the wire**. You improve **reliability** by repeating readings and calculating a mean, and improve **accuracy** by using better equipment and careful technique. **Resolution** is the smallest change an instrument can show, so meters with smaller scale divisions give better results.

bullets: Resistance **increases** with length (directly proportional).
Resistance **decreases** as cross-sectional area increases.
Resistance depends on **material**; constantan has a higher resistance than copper for the same size.
Resistance of a metal **increases** with temperature.
To test thickness: use wires of the same length and material but different diameter.
A thicker-wire graph has a **smaller gradient** than a thin-wire graph.
Heating elements use high-resistance wire; connecting cables use low-resistance copper.
core.h: Effect of thickness and other factors
core.p: The resistance of a wire depends on its **length**, its **cross-sectional area (thickness)**, its **material** and its **temperature**. For a given material, a **longer** wire has more resistance and a **thicker** wire has less resistance. A graph of resistance against length for a thicker wire is a **less steep straight line** than for a thin wire because each centimetre of thick wire has a lower resistance. Keeping the other factors constant is how you test one factor at a time.

bullets: Series: **R total = R1 + R2**.
Parallel: total resistance is **smaller than the smallest** resistor.
Adding resistors in series is similar to **increasing length**.
Adding resistors in parallel is similar to **increasing cross-sectional area**.
The same circuit (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel) is used for each combination.
Compare calculated and measured totals to check your results.
Series: the same current; parallel: the same p.d. across each branch.
core.h: Resistors in series and parallel (related part of the practical)
core.p: The AQA practical on resistance also covers combining resistors. When resistors are connected **in series** the total resistance is the **sum of the individual resistances**, because the current has to pass through each one in turn, like making the wire longer. When resistors are connected **in parallel** the total resistance is **less than the smallest individual resistance**, because there are more paths for the current, like making the wire thicker. You test this by measuring V and I for each combination and calculating R = V / I.

bullets: For a 'describe the method' question, include: circuit (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel), how the length is varied and measured, how R is calculated, repeats and mean.
Name the **independent, dependent and control variables** correctly.
Explain **why** a control matters, e.g. 'so the temperature does not change the resistance'.
Know **how to reduce error** and how to improve reliability.
A straight line through the origin means **direct proportionality**.
Use **gradient** to find resistance per unit length.
Write units and show working.
core.p: Questions on this practical test the method, the variables, the graph and the explanation. Expect a **6-mark method question** (describe how you would investigate...), **graph plotting and gradient calculations**, **identification of variables**, and **evaluation** of errors. Marks are awarded for a circuit that is complete and correct, a clear sequence in the method, a statement of the control variables with the reason, and a safe approach.

exam: 6 marks (describe a method): circuit with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel; how length is varied and measured; how R is calculated; control variables; repeats and mean; safety.
Variable questions: independent = length; dependent = resistance (from V and I); control = material, thickness, p.d., temperature.
Calculation: write R = V / I, substitute with units, give the answer in ohms.
Graph: resistance on y axis, length on x axis, axis labels with units, plot carefully, ruler line through the origin.
Conclusion: 'resistance is directly proportional to the length of the wire'.
Explanation: link length to number of ions, collisions and resistance.
Safety: low p.d., switch off between readings, do not touch the hot wire.
Error questions: name the error (random or systematic), then how to reduce it (repeat, mean, zero check, better resolution).
Gradient: use a large triangle on the line; gradient = change in R / change in L, with units (ohm per cm or per m).
Predictions: use the line to find an unknown value; show the construction on the graph.
Command words: **describe** = say what you would do; **explain** = give the reason; **evaluate** = weigh strengths and weaknesses.

mistakes.w: Resistance increases with length, so it is proportional.

mistakes.r: Switch the circuit off between readings and use a low current so the wire does not heat up.
mistakes.w: Keep the temperature the same by keeping the room cool.

mistakes.w: Resistance is measured by the ammeter.

mistakes.w: The wire gets hot because of friction.

mistakes.w: Control variables are the length and the current.

summary: You need to be able to carry out and describe the required practical that investigates how the resistance of a wire depends on its length, using an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel, calculating R = V / I and plotting resistance against length. This matters because it is a core required practical, it tests control variables, graph skills and explanations in terms of electrons and ions, and the result (resistance directly proportional to length) is a regular exam question.

terms.d: A measure of how difficult it is for current to flow; resistance = potential difference / current, measured in ohms.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.

A variable that is kept the same so that the test is fair.

An instrument that measures potential difference, connected in parallel across a component.

An unpredictable error that causes readings to vary above and below the true value; reduced by repeating and averaging.

worked.ans: The resistances are 2.0, 4.0 and 10.0 ohms. Resistance is directly proportional to length (0.10 ohm per cm, a gradient of 10 ohms per metre), so a 70 cm length has a resistance of 7.0 ohms.
worked.q: A student measures the p.d. across and current through different lengths of a wire. At 20 cm: V = 0.50 V, I = 0.25 A. At 40 cm: V = 0.80 V, I = 0.20 A. At 100 cm: V = 1.50 V, I = 0.15 A. Calculate the resistance at each length, state the relationship and predict the resistance of 70 cm. (5 marks)
steps: Resistance per cm = 2.0 / 20 = 0.10 ohm per cm in each case, so R is proportional to L.

worked.ans: The anomaly is 7.4 ohms; the mean of the remaining values is 6.0 ohms. The anomaly may be due to heating of the wire or poor contact at a crocodile clip.
worked.q: For a 60 cm length, three repeat readings of resistance are 6.1, 5.9 and 6.0 ohms and a fourth is 7.4 ohms. Identify the anomaly and calculate the mean. Suggest one possible cause of the anomaly. (3 marks)
steps: 7.4 ohms is far from the other three, so it is the anomalous result.
Possible cause: the wire heated up, or the clip was not in contact at the correct position.

worked.ans: Connect the test wire in series with a cell, a switch and an ammeter and connect a voltmeter in parallel across the wire. Use a metre rule to set the length between two crocodile clips, starting at 10 cm. Close the switch, record the current and the p.d., then open the switch to stop the wire from heating. Increase the length in 10 cm steps up to 100 cm. Repeat and calculate a mean. For each length calculate resistance using R = V / I. Keep the same wire and the same p.d. as control variables. Plot resistance against length: a straight line through the origin shows that resistance is directly proportional to length.
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length. (6 marks)
steps: Set up a series circuit with a cell, switch, ammeter and the test wire; connect a voltmeter in parallel across the wire.
Tape the wire to a metre rule and use crocodile clips to select the length.
Close the switch, record the p.d. and current, then open the switch to avoid heating.
Change the length in steps of 10 cm and repeat.
Calculate R = V / I for each length and take a mean of repeats.
Control wire material, thickness, p.d. and temperature; plot R against L.
